add_subtopics.title: Other stacks and provider portability
add_subtopics.body:
Not every customer writes Python, and not every customer will stay with one model vendor. An FDE should know the main options outside the tools in this lesson.

Other languages. In TypeScript, the Vercel AI SDK gives one interface for many providers, with streaming and tool calling (see the frontend topic). On .NET and Java, Microsoft's Agent Framework and Semantic Kernel are common, and Spring AI fits teams already on Spring. All of them wrap the same loop you wrote by hand.

Cloud agent platforms. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Google's Vertex AI Agent Builder host agents, memory and tool access inside the customer's cloud account. They suit customers who want one bill, one security review and managed scaling, at the price of tying the agent to that cloud.

Typed output libraries. Pydantic AI and Instructor make the model return a Pydantic object and retry when the output does not fit the schema. They are small and easy to review.

Gateways. LiteLLM presents many providers behind one OpenAI-style call, so switching a model is a string change. It also does routing, keys, budgets and fallbacks. Use it when the customer wants to avoid lock-in or to compare vendors.

DSPy. Instead of hand-writing prompts, you declare inputs and outputs in code and let DSPy search for better prompts against your eval set. It is worth a look when you already have a good eval set and a prompt that is hard to improve by hand.

Whichever you pick, keep your tools, prompts and evals in plain files, so moving to another stack means changing a thin layer, not rewriting the project.
add_subtopics.example: A Dutch manufacturer's platform team writes Java, and its security team only approves models served from its own cloud region. The FDE builds the agent on Spring AI, puts LiteLLM in front as a gateway with a fallback model, and keeps the tool definitions and the 80-question eval set as JSON files. Six months later they switch models by editing one line of gateway config and re-running the evals.

# Provider portability: one call shape, many providers (LiteLLM), and typed output (Instructor)
import instructor, litellm
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: str
    urgent: bool

# LiteLLM: switch provider by changing the model string (names here are placeholders)
reply = litellm.completion(model="PROVIDER/MODEL",
                           messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Printer on floor 3 is jammed"}])
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)

# Instructor: ask for a Pydantic object and get one, with automatic retries on bad output
client = instructor.from_provider("PROVIDER/MODEL")
ticket = client.chat.completions.create(
    response_model=Ticket, max_retries=2,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Printer on floor 3 is jammed, urgent!"}])
print(ticket)                                            # category='hardware' urgent=True
# Not run here: needs provider keys. The two libraries were checked only for syntax.

replace_subtopics.title: The core loop every framework wraps
replace_subtopics.body:
Before comparing frameworks, write the loop yourself once. You describe tools with a name, a description and a JSON Schema for their inputs (see the tools concept). You send the conversation and the tools to the model. If the response's stop reason is tool use, you run each requested tool, append the results, and call the model again. Otherwise you are done.

That is the whole agent. Everything else, including retries, memory, streaming, logging and limits on how many steps may run, is added around this loop.

A plain loop has real strengths. You see the exact messages sent, you can test each tool as a normal function, and there are no hidden prompts. For many enterprise tasks this plus good tools and evaluations is all you need.

Two details make the loop safe. First, when a tool fails, do not crash: return the error to the model as a tool_result block with is_error set to true, so it can try again or explain. Second, stop reasons are not only tool_use and end_turn. A reply can stop with max_tokens (it was cut off, so raise the limit), pause_turn (a server-side tool needs another turn, so send the conversation back) or refusal (the model declined). And check the step cap: if the loop ends because the 10 steps ran out, there may be no text answer at all.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer wants a support assistant that looks up orders and starts returns. The FDE writes a 40-line loop with two tools, get_order and create_return, plus a cap of 10 steps. Every call is logged to the customer's existing logging system. The whole thing is easy for the customer's two Python developers to read.
replace_subtopics.code:
import json, anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
tools = [{"name": "get_order", "description": "Look up an order by its id.",
          "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                           "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                           "required": ["order_id"]}}]

def run_tool(name: str, args: dict) -> dict:
    if name == "get_order":
        return {"order_id": args["order_id"], "status": "shipped", "eta": "2026-10-02"}
    return {"error": f"unknown tool {name}"}

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order 4471?"}]
answer = "(no answer: step limit reached)"
for _ in range(10):                                   # hard cap on steps
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":
        results = []
        for b in resp.content:
            if b.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            try:
                out = run_tool(b.name, b.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                                "content": json.dumps(out)})
            except Exception as e:                    # tell the model, do not crash
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                                "content": f"Tool failed: {e}", "is_error": True})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
        continue
    if resp.stop_reason == "pause_turn":              # server tool paused: send it back
        continue
    text = "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
    if resp.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
        text += " [cut off: raise max_tokens]"
    elif resp.stop_reason == "refusal":
        text = text or "(the model declined this request)"
    answer = text or answer
    break

print(answer)

replace_subtopics.title: LangChain and LlamaIndex: integrations and data
replace_subtopics.body:
LangChain is a large Python and JavaScript ecosystem. Its main value is a common interface over many model providers and a big library of integrations: document loaders, vector stores, retrievers, output parsers and tools. Recent versions build their agent features on LangGraph. Its companion product LangSmith offers tracing and evaluation.

LlamaIndex focuses on connecting LLMs to data. It gives you readers for many file types and sources, ways to split and index documents, and query engines that do retrieval plus answering in a few lines. It also has agent and workflow features, but it is chosen most often for RAG-heavy projects (see the rag concept).

Both move fast, and their APIs have changed a lot between versions. Pin versions, read the current docs rather than old blog posts, and wrap framework calls behind your own small functions so you can swap them later.

A note on versions: LangChain 1.0 (late 2025) is built around create_agent, which runs the tool loop for you and accepts middleware (small hooks that can trim history, add approval steps or redact data). Older blog posts that use AgentExecutor or LLMChain describe legacy code, so check which version you are reading before copying anything.
replace_subtopics.example: A law firm wants to ask questions over 8,000 engagement letters stored in SharePoint. LlamaIndex's loaders and indexing get a working prototype in a day. The team keeps LlamaIndex for ingestion and retrieval, but writes the final answering step and citation formatting in plain code so they control the prompt exactly.

replace_subtopics.title: LangGraph: state, branches and checkpoints
replace_subtopics.body:
LangGraph, from the LangChain team, models an agent or workflow as a graph. Nodes are functions that read and update a shared state object. Edges say what runs next, and conditional edges choose the next node from the state.

Its strongest feature is checkpointing. After each step the state can be saved to memory or a database, keyed by a thread id. That lets a flow pause for a human approval and resume hours later, recover after a crash, or let a user go back to an earlier step. It also supports streaming and multi-agent setups.

The price is more concepts to learn and more code than a simple loop. It pays off when the process is long-running, branching or needs people in the middle.

The current style for human approval is interrupt(). You call it inside a node, and the graph stops there and saves its state. Later you resume with Command(resume=value), and interrupt() returns that value inside the node. The older compile-time option interrupt_before still works, but it is mostly used for debugging.

The checkpointer must be durable. InMemorySaver keeps state only in the running process, so a restart loses every paused claim and the "resume the next day" story breaks. Use SqliteSaver for a single machine or PostgresSaver for production. For what an agent should remember across sessions, see the agent memory topic.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's refund flow: an LLM assesses a claim, small refunds go to a refund step, large ones to escalation. Refunds must be approved by a person. With LangGraph the graph pauses before send_refund, the claim state is saved under the claim id, and when a handler clicks approve the next day the graph resumes from exactly that point.

import sqlite3
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver

class Claim(TypedDict):
    claim_id: str
    amount: float
    decision: str
    approved: bool

def assess(s: Claim) -> dict:          # in practice: an LLM call
    return {"decision": "refund" if s["amount"] < 500 else "escalate"}

def approve(s: Claim) -> dict:
    # interrupt() pauses here and returns whatever the human sends back
    answer = interrupt({"question": f"Approve refund of {s['amount']} for claim {s['claim_id']}?"})
    return {"approved": bool(answer)}

def send_refund(s: Claim) -> dict:
    print("refund sent" if s["approved"] else "refund rejected")
    return {}

def escalate(s: Claim) -> dict:
    print("escalated to a senior handler")
    return {}

g = StateGraph(Claim)
for name, fn in [("assess", assess), ("approve", approve),
                 ("send_refund", send_refund), ("escalate", escalate)]:
    g.add_node(name, fn)
g.add_edge(START, "assess")
g.add_conditional_edges("assess", lambda s: s["decision"],
                        {"refund": "approve", "escalate": "escalate"})
g.add_edge("approve", "send_refund")
g.add_edge("send_refund", END)
g.add_edge("escalate", END)

# A durable checkpointer: the paused claim survives a restart (use PostgresSaver in production)
saver = SqliteSaver(sqlite3.connect("claims.db", check_same_thread=False))
app = g.compile(checkpointer=saver)
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "claim-981"}}

first = app.invoke({"claim_id": "981", "amount": 120.0, "decision": "", "approved": False}, cfg)
print("paused with:", first["__interrupt__"][0].value)      # the graph is now saved and waiting
# ...next day, possibly a different process...
app.invoke(Command(resume=True), cfg)                        # the human said yes
# Output:
# paused with: {'question': 'Approve refund of 120.0 for claim 981?'}
# refund sent

replace_subtopics.title: Claude Agent SDK and other agent SDKs
replace_subtopics.body:
The Claude Agent SDK, from Anthropic, exposes the agent harness that powers Claude Code as a library for Python and TypeScript. You give it a prompt and options, and it runs the loop for you with built-in tools for reading and editing files, running shell commands, searching and fetching web pages. It supports MCP servers for your own tools (see the mcp concept), subagents, hooks that run your code before or after tool calls, and permission settings that limit what the agent may do.

It fits tasks where an agent works through files and commands over many steps: coding, operations runbooks, research over a folder of reports. For a simple chat with two API tools, the plain SDK loop is smaller.

Other vendors and communities offer similar kits, for example the OpenAI Agents SDK, Google's Agent Development Kit, Microsoft's agent frameworks, CrewAI and Pydantic AI. They differ in which models they favour, how they handle multi-agent setups and how much they hide. Judge them the same way: what work do they remove, and what do they hide from you?

Three more features you will use. A PreToolUse hook runs your code before a tool runs and can block it, for example refusing any shell command that contains rm -rf. Custom tools can run inside your own process: write a function with the @tool decorator and wrap it with create_sdk_mcp_server, with no separate server to deploy. And ClaudeSDKClient keeps one session open for a multi-turn chat, while query() starts a fresh one each time.
replace_subtopics.example: A utility's IT team wants a daily job that reads yesterday's application logs, groups errors, and writes a short report to a shared folder. The FDE uses the Claude Agent SDK with only Read, Grep, Glob and Write tools allowed, a working directory limited to the logs and reports folders, and a cap on turns. No shell access is granted, which makes the security review simple.
replace_subtopics.code:
# pip install claude-agent-sdk
import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    system_prompt="You write short daily error reports for the IT team.",
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Write"],   # no shell access
    permission_mode="acceptEdits",                       # may write files without asking
    cwd="/srv/ops-agent",                                # working folder
    max_turns=20,                                        # stop runaway loops
)

async def main():
    prompt = "Group yesterday's errors in logs/app.log and write reports/daily.md"
    async for message in query(prompt=prompt, options=options):
        print(message)                                   # stream progress

asyncio.run(main())

# --- Hooks, in-process tools and multi-turn sessions ---
import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import (ClaudeAgentOptions, ClaudeSDKClient, HookMatcher,
                              create_sdk_mcp_server, tool)

# 1. A hook that runs before every Bash call and blocks dangerous commands
async def block_rm(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    command = input_data["tool_input"].get("command", "")
    if "rm -rf" in command:
        return {"hookSpecificOutput": {
            "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
            "permissionDecision": "deny",
            "permissionDecisionReason": "Deleting files is not allowed here"}}
    return {}                                            # empty means: carry on

# 2. Your own tool, served in-process (no separate MCP server to run)
@tool("get_order", "Look up an order by id", {"order_id": str})
async def get_order(args):
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"Order {args['order_id']}: shipped"}]}

shop = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="shop", version="1.0.0", tools=[get_order])

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    mcp_servers={"shop": shop},
    allowed_tools=["mcp__shop__get_order", "Bash"],
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="Bash", hooks=[block_rm])]},
    max_turns=10,
)

# 3. ClaudeSDKClient keeps one session open for a multi-turn conversation
async def main():
    async with ClaudeSDKClient(options=options) as client:
        await client.query("Where is order 4471?")
        async for message in client.receive_response():
            print(message)
        await client.query("And order 4472?")            # remembers the conversation
        async for message in client.receive_response():
            print(message)

# asyncio.run(main())   # needs the Claude Code CLI installed and an API key
# The hook logic was run alone: rm -rf gives 'deny', ls gives {} (allowed).

replace_subtopics.title: Side by side comparison
replace_subtopics.body:
The table below is a rough guide. All of these tools change quickly, so check current documentation before a decision, and build a small spike with real data.

Notice that the options are not exclusive. A common, healthy pattern is plain code for the main loop, LlamaIndex or LangChain only for a loader or two, and LangGraph only for the one flow that needs pausing and approval.

Whatever you choose, add tracing so every prompt, tool call and result is visible, and keep evaluations independent of the framework, so you can switch later and prove nothing got worse.

Add one more column when you compare: what it costs to leave. A plain loop costs almost nothing to migrate. A framework with its own state format, prompt templates and tracing needs a rewrite of those parts. A managed cloud agent platform is the hardest to leave, because your agent's memory and tools live in it. Ask this before the customer commits. For tracing tools that work with any framework, see the LLM observability topic.

add_subtopics.title: Loading structured data and keeping the graph fresh
add_subtopics.body:
The lesson says a good middle path is to seed the graph from structured data the customer already has. Here is how, and how to keep the graph correct afterwards.

Bulk loading. An ERP or HR table is already a list of facts: supplier, part, country. Export it as CSV and use LOAD CSV in Cypher, which reads each row and runs MERGE on it. Put the file in Neo4j's import folder, and use MERGE on a unique key (with a uniqueness constraint) so running the load twice does not create duplicates. For millions of rows, the neo4j-admin import tool is much faster, but it works on an empty database.

Provenance. Every edge should carry a source property (a file name, a table name, a page) and a load time. Provenance lets the model cite sources, and lets you find and remove exactly what one document said.

Incremental updates. Documents change. The simplest safe method is: extract the new facts first, then in one transaction delete all edges whose source is that document, and load the new ones. Extracting first means a failed extraction leaves the old facts in place. Afterwards remove nodes that have no relationships left.

Scheduling. Run a nightly job (cron or an orchestrator such as Airflow). For files, compare a hash of the content with the stored hash and reprocess only what changed. For ERP tables, reload with LOAD CSV on the same schedule, or filter by an updated_at column.

Keep watching. Count nodes and edges per source each day. A sudden drop or jump usually means a broken export, not a real change.
add_subtopics.example: A manufacturer loads its supplier_parts table (9,400 rows) with LOAD CSV in about a minute and gets 1,900 Company nodes, 7,200 Part nodes and 9,400 SUPPLIES edges, each stamped source erp:supplier_parts. When contract_2291.pdf is renegotiated, the nightly job notices a new file hash, extracts the new facts, deletes the 6 edges with that source, and loads 5 new ones. A daily count shows SUPPLIES edges fell from 9,400 to 40 one Monday: the ERP export had failed, and the alert caught it before anyone queried bad data.

replace_subtopics.title: Graph databases and Cypher
replace_subtopics.body:
You could store triples in a normal SQL table, but questions that follow many hops need many self-joins and get slow and hard to write. A graph database stores each node with direct links to its neighbours, so following connections is cheap.

Neo4j is the most widely known graph database. It uses a query language called Cypher, where you draw the pattern you want with ASCII art: (a)-[:SUPPLIES]->(b). MATCH finds patterns, MERGE creates nodes or edges only if they do not already exist, and RETURN picks the output. Other options include Amazon Neptune, Memgraph and graph features in some relational and multi-model databases.

For an FDE, the high-level point is simple: a graph database makes variable-length, many-hop questions easy to express and fast to run. You still need indexes on the properties you look up, such as names or IDs.

Some habits that avoid trouble. Use a uniqueness constraint (CREATE CONSTRAINT ... REQUIRE x.name IS UNIQUE) instead of a plain index: it speeds lookups and also stops duplicates. Be careful with MERGE: MERGE (c:Entity {name: 'X', type: 'Company'}) creates a second node if an existing X has a different type, because MERGE matches on every property you list. MERGE on the key only and use SET for the other properties. Real labels such as :Company and :Part are also better than one generic :Entity with a type property, because the database can index and check each label.

From Python, create one driver (GraphDatabase.driver with the URI and auth), run queries with execute_query, choose read routing for read-only questions, and pass values as parameters. Never build Cypher with f-strings from user text, because that opens the door to injection.

If the customer will not run Neo4j, multi-hop questions still work in Postgres with WITH RECURSIVE, or with the Apache AGE extension that adds Cypher to Postgres. That is fine for a few hops on modest data.
replace_subtopics.example: The question 'which products are affected if Hollin Castings stops shipping?' becomes a single Cypher pattern from the company through SUPPLIES and PART_OF to products. In SQL this would be two joins today and more as the chain grows, for example when parts go into sub-assemblies that go into products.
replace_subtopics.code:
// Uniqueness constraint: fast lookups and no duplicates
CREATE CONSTRAINT company_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (c:Company) REQUIRE c.name IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT part_name    IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Part)    REQUIRE p.name IS UNIQUE;

// MERGE on the key only, then SET the other properties (real labels, not a generic :Entity)
MERGE (c:Company {name: 'Hollin Castings'}) SET c.country = 'Japan'
MERGE (p:Part {name: 'Brake caliper B7'})
MERGE (c)-[:SUPPLIES {source: 'contract_2291.pdf'}]->(p);

// Which products depend on this company, through any number of PART_OF hops?
MATCH (c:Company {name: 'Hollin Castings'})-[:SUPPLIES]->(part)
      -[:PART_OF*1..4]->(product:Product)
RETURN DISTINCT product.name AS affected_product;

# --- From Python: one driver, read routing, parameters (not f-strings) ---
from neo4j import GraphDatabase

# Setup: one driver for the whole app, credentials from the environment in real code
driver = GraphDatabase.driver("neo4j://graph-host:7687", auth=("readonly_user", "PASSWORD"))

def products_hit(company: str):
    # Parameters ($company) are sent separately from the query text: safe against injection.
    # Never build Cypher with f-strings from user text.
    records, _, _ = driver.execute_query(
        "MATCH (c:Company {name: $company})-[:SUPPLIES]->(:Part)-[:PART_OF*1..4]->(p:Product) "
        "RETURN DISTINCT p.name AS product",
        company=company, routing_="r")            # "r" = read: goes to a read replica in a cluster
    return [r["product"] for r in records]

-- --- No graph database? The same walk in SQL (run here on SQLite; Postgres is the same) ---

--     SELECT parent, 1 FROM part_of WHERE child = 'Brake caliper B7'
--     UNION ALL
--     SELECT p.parent, up.depth + 1 FROM part_of p JOIN up ON p.child = up.name
--     WHERE up.depth < 4)

replace_subtopics.title: GraphRAG for multi-hop questions
replace_subtopics.body:
A multi-hop question needs several facts chained together. 'Which products depend on suppliers in Kumamoto?' needs supplier to site, supplier to part, and part to product. Vector search may return a chunk about each, or may not, because none of them looks very similar to the question.

A typical graph-based retrieval step works like this. Find the entities named in the question (Kumamoto), look them up in the graph, walk the relevant relationships a few hops, collect the paths and the source text behind each edge, and give those to the LLM. The model then writes an answer and cites the sources. An LLM can also translate questions into Cypher, but check generated queries carefully and restrict them to read-only access.

Microsoft Research's GraphRAG approach adds another idea: it groups the graph into communities of closely linked entities and writes a summary for each. Those summaries help with broad questions such as 'what are the main risks across all supplier contracts?', which no single chunk can answer. This indexing is costly, so it fits large, fairly stable collections.

Two gaps to close. First, where does the starting entity come from? A user types free text, not a clean node name. Entity linking finds it: build a full-text or vector index over node names inside the graph and search it with the question, keeping the best match only if its score is high enough. An alternative is Text2Cypher, where the model writes the Cypher itself. Put the graph schema in the prompt, run the query as a read-only user, and check it with EXPLAIN before running it.

Second, the traversal must match the question. The code below now follows PART_OF up to four hops (*1..4), the same as the Cypher earlier. A single hop would miss parts inside sub-assemblies.

Finally, Microsoft's GraphRAG offers two search modes: local search starts from entities and their neighbours for specific questions, and global search uses community summaries for broad questions. Because its indexing is expensive, lighter variants exist, such as LazyGraphRAG (delays most LLM work until query time) and LightRAG (a simpler graph and retrieval design).
replace_subtopics.example: After a flood warning, a planner asks which cars could be delayed. The system finds Kumamoto, walks to three suppliers, seven parts and two products, and passes those 12 facts plus their contract snippets to the model. The answer names both products, lists the parts and links each claim to its source document. Plain vector RAG on the same question returned only one of the two products in testing.
replace_subtopics.code:
import re

def find_entity(driver, question: str) -> str | None:
    """Entity linking: turn free text into a node name using a full-text index in the graph.
    Setup once: CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX entity_names IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Company|Site) ON EACH [n.name]"""
    words = " ".join(re.findall(r"[A-Za-z0-9]+", question))       # strip Lucene special characters
    records, _, _ = driver.execute_query(
        "CALL db.index.fulltext.queryNodes('entity_names', $q) YIELD node, score "
        "RETURN node.name AS name, score ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 1", q=words, routing_="r")
    return records[0]["name"] if records and records[0]["score"] > 1.0 else None

def graph_context(driver, place: str) -> str:
    records, _, _ = driver.execute_query("""
        MATCH (s)-[:LOCATED_IN]->(:Site {name: $place}),
              path = (s)-[:SUPPLIES]->(part)-[:PART_OF*1..4]->(product:Product)   // same depth as before
        RETURN s.name AS supplier, part.name AS part, product.name AS product,
               [r IN relationships(path) | r.source] AS sources
        LIMIT 50""", place=place, routing_="r")                # read-only, bounded
    return "\n".join(f"{r['supplier']} supplies {r['part']}, used in {r['product']} "
                     f"(sources: {', '.join(r['sources'])})" for r in records)

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    place = find_entity(driver, question)
    if place is None:
        return "I could not find a matching place in the graph."
    facts = graph_context(driver, place)
    prompt = (f"Answer using only these facts and cite sources.\n\nFACTS:\n{facts}"
              f"\n\nQUESTION: {question}")
    msg = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=800,
                                 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return "".join(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text")

# Text2Cypher (for open questions): put the schema in the prompt, run as a READ-ONLY user,
# and check the query with EXPLAIN before running it:
#   driver.execute_query("EXPLAIN " + generated_cypher)   # fails fast on bad syntax
# Checked with a fake driver and a fake model client (no live Neo4j): the prompt held the
# supplier, part, product and sources, and the answer was returned as joined text.

add_subtopics.title: Evaluating voice and vision systems
add_subtopics.body:
Contact centres and claims teams buy on numbers, so you need to report the right ones. (For how to run simulated callers and live pilots, see the Voice topic; for production traces and sampling, see LLM observability.)

Voice metrics.
- Task completion: the share of calls where the caller's goal was met (leak reported, appointment moved). Judge it against the tool calls and the final state, not only the transcript.
- Containment rate: the share of calls finished without a human. Its opposite is the transfer rate. High containment is only good if completion is also high, because a caller who gives up and hangs up is contained but not helped.
- Average handle time (AHT): the mean call length in seconds. Compare it with the human baseline.
- Per-stage latency percentiles: for each stage (end of turn, STT, LLM first token, TTS first audio) report p50 and p95, never the average. One turn of 2.6 seconds ruins a call even when the median is 1 second.
- Field accuracy: for names, meter numbers and dates, the share captured exactly right.

Vision metrics. Score field by field against hand-labelled truth. A receipt total that is wrong by 9 cents is one wrong field, and a wrong total matters more than a wrong shop name. Also track how often the model says 'unclear' when it should, and the share of images sent to a person.

Build the test set from real, hard examples: noisy calls, accents, blurry and rotated photos. Re-run it whenever the prompt, the model or the STT vendor changes, and keep a small human-labelled sample for spot checks.
add_subtopics.example: A water utility pilots its leak-reporting agent on 5 test calls (a tiny set, for illustration). Completion is 60 percent, containment 80 percent and AHT 125 seconds against a human average of 240. The p95 turn latency is 2,600 ms while the p50 is 1,000 ms, which points to one slow tool call. On the photo side, the receipt reader gets the date right in 100 percent of test images but the total in only 50 percent, so totals go to a person for review.

# Score simulated or real calls. Each record is one call outcome (made-up sample data).
calls = [
    {"solved": True,  "transferred": False, "seconds": 140, "turn_ms": [900, 1100, 1000]},
    {"solved": True,  "transferred": False, "seconds": 95,  "turn_ms": [800, 1200, 950]},
    {"solved": False, "transferred": True,  "seconds": 210, "turn_ms": [1000, 2600, 1300]},
    {"solved": True,  "transferred": False, "seconds": 120, "turn_ms": [850, 900, 1050]},
    {"solved": False, "transferred": False, "seconds": 60,  "turn_ms": [950, 1400, 1150]},
]
n = len(calls)
task_completion = sum(c["solved"] for c in calls) / n
containment = sum(not c["transferred"] for c in calls) / n      # finished without a human
transfer_rate = 1 - containment
aht = sum(c["seconds"] for c in calls) / n                       # average handle time

all_turns = sorted(t for c in calls for t in c["turn_ms"])
def pct(p): return all_turns[min(len(all_turns) - 1, int(p * len(all_turns)))]

print(f"task completion {task_completion:.0%}, containment {containment:.0%}, "
      f"transfer {transfer_rate:.0%}, AHT {aht:.0f}s")
print(f"turn latency p50 {pct(0.50)} ms, p95 {pct(0.95)} ms")

# Vision: field-level accuracy against hand-labelled truth
truth = [{"total": "41.20", "date": "2026-09-01"}, {"total": "9.99", "date": "2026-09-03"}]
pred  = [{"total": "41.20", "date": "2026-09-01"}, {"total": "9.90", "date": "2026-09-03"}]
for field in ("total", "date"):
    acc = sum(t[field] == p[field] for t, p in zip(truth, pred)) / len(truth)
    print(f"field {field}: {acc:.0%} correct")
# Output:
# task completion 60%, containment 80%, transfer 20%, AHT 125s
# turn latency p50 1000 ms, p95 2600 ms
# field total: 50% correct
# field date: 100% correct

replace_subtopics.title: Sending images to an LLM
replace_subtopics.body:
With a vision-capable model you add an image to the message as a content block, next to your text instruction. The image can be sent as base64 data or, with some APIs, as a URL. The model sees it as part of the prompt.

Images cost tokens, roughly in proportion to their pixel size, so resize large photos to what the task needs. Very small text, dense tables, exact counting and precise positions are known weak spots, so test those cases carefully.

For extraction tasks, combine vision with the document-pipeline habits from the docai concept: a fixed schema, validation and human review. For judgement tasks, such as 'is this damage consistent with the claim?', treat the model's answer as a suggestion for a person, not a decision.

Cost. For Claude, an image costs roughly width x height / 750 tokens, and very large images are scaled down anyway, so resize the long edge to about 1,568 pixels yourself and save upload time. A 3,000 x 2,000 photo becomes about 2,185 tokens. You can send several images in one message: label each ('Image 1:', 'Image 2:') so your question can refer to them. Some APIs accept a URL instead of base64. For video, send sampled frames as images, for example one every two seconds.

Image embeddings. A CLIP-style model turns images and text into vectors in the same space. That gives you photo search ('water stain on a ceiling') without an LLM call, and a cheap fraud check: two different claims with nearly identical photos usually mean a reused picture. Set the similarity threshold using known duplicates.
replace_subtopics.example: A home insurer receives phone photos of water damage. The model is asked to describe the damaged areas, list visible items and flag if the photo seems to show a different room from the claim description. Adjusters see the summary next to the photos, saving them a few minutes per claim, and they make the decision.
replace_subtopics.code:
import anthropic, base64
from PIL import Image

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def image_tokens(path: str) -> int:
    """Rough cost estimate for Claude: width x height / 750, after shrinking the long edge to 1568 px."""
    w, h = Image.open(path).size
    scale = min(1.0, 1568 / max(w, h))
    return round(w * scale * h * scale / 750)

def shrink(path: str, out: str, long_edge: int = 1568):
    img = Image.open(path)
    img.thumbnail((long_edge, long_edge))            # keeps the aspect ratio
    img.save(out, quality=90)

def block(path: str) -> dict:
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        data = base64.standard_b64encode(f.read()).decode()
    return {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/jpeg", "data": data}}

# An image can also come from a URL (the API fetches it): {"type": "url", "url": "https://..."}
url_block = {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "url", "url": "https://example.com/photo.jpg"}}

# Several images: label each one so you can refer to it in the question
content = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Image 1:"}, block("claim_7781_kitchen.jpg"),
    {"type": "text", "text": "Image 2:"}, block("claim_7781_ceiling.jpg"),
    {"type": "text", "text": "Do these two photos show the same room? Answer yes, no or unclear, with one reason."},
]
msg = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=300,
                             messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}])
print("".join(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text"))    # a suggestion for the adjuster

# Video: the API takes images, not video files. Sample one frame every 2 seconds, then send
# the frames as labelled images ("Frame 1 (0s):", "Frame 2 (2s):" ...).

# --- Image embeddings for search and reused-photo checks (CLIP style) ---
# pip install sentence-transformers pillow
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
from PIL import Image

model = SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")          # embeds images and text into one space

paths = ["claim_7781_kitchen.jpg", "claim_8120_kitchen.jpg", "claim_9002_garage.jpg"]
vecs = model.encode([Image.open(p) for p in paths], convert_to_tensor=True)

# Photo search: find the images closest to a text query
q = model.encode("water stain on a kitchen ceiling", convert_to_tensor=True)
print(util.cos_sim(q, vecs))

# Reused-photo check: two different claims with a near-identical picture is a fraud signal
for i in range(len(paths)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(paths)):
        sim = util.cos_sim(vecs[i], vecs[j]).item()
        if sim > 0.95:                                # tune this threshold on known duplicates
            print(f"possible reused photo: {paths[i]} and {paths[j]} (similarity {sim:.2f})")
# The token estimate was run: a 3000 x 2000 image gives 2185. The API and CLIP code was checked
# for syntax only, since it needs a key and a model download.

replace_subtopics.title: Speech-to-text and measuring it
replace_subtopics.body:
STT models take audio and return text, often with timestamps per word. Whisper is a well-known open model you can run yourself; many cloud providers and specialist companies offer STT APIs, including streaming versions that return partial text while the person is still speaking.

Phone audio is harder than studio audio. It is usually sampled at 8 kHz, has background noise and cross-talk, and callers say names, account numbers and addresses that general models get wrong. Many services let you add a list of expected words (sometimes called custom vocabulary or keyword boosting), which helps with product names.

The standard quality measure is word error rate (WER): the number of word substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by the number of words in a correct reference transcript. Measure it on the customer's own recordings, and separately check the fields that matter, like account numbers, because one wrong digit is a failure even if WER looks good. Diarization, which labels who spoke when, is useful for call analytics.

A trap in the code below: Whisper returns punctuation, capital letters and digits ('Hi, my meter number is 4412') while a hand-typed reference often spells the numbers out ('four four one two'). Compared raw, the WER looks terrible even though nothing was misheard: 0.429 for this sentence. Normalise both sides first: lowercase, strip punctuation, and turn digits into words. After that the WER is 0.0. Always score against the same normalisation you will use in production.
replace_subtopics.example: A utility tests two STT options on 100 recorded customer calls with hand-made transcripts. Overall WER is similar, around 12 and 14 percent, but one option gets the 10-digit meter number fully right in 91 of 100 calls and the other in 78. The team picks the first and adds read-back confirmation of meter numbers.
replace_subtopics.code:
# pip install openai-whisper jiwer   (Whisper also needs ffmpeg installed)
import re
import whisper, jiwer

model = whisper.load_model("small")                  # sizes: tiny ... large
result = model.transcribe("call_0193.wav", language="en")
print("transcript:", result["text"])
for seg in result["segments"]:                         # timestamps per segment
    print(f"{seg['start']:6.1f}s  {seg['text']}")

# Normalise BOTH texts before scoring
DIGITS = "zero one two three four five six seven eight nine".split()
def digits_to_words(text: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"\d", lambda m: " " + DIGITS[int(m.group())] + " ", text)   # 4412 -> four four one two

normalise = jiwer.Compose([jiwer.ToLowerCase(), jiwer.RemovePunctuation(),
                           jiwer.RemoveMultipleSpaces(), jiwer.Strip()])
def clean(text: str) -> str:
    return normalise(digits_to_words(text))

reference  = "hi my meter number is four four one two and the power is out"
hypothesis = "Hi, my meter number is 4412 and the power is out."      # what Whisper really returns
print("raw WER:       ", round(jiwer.wer(reference, hypothesis), 3))
print("normalised WER:", round(jiwer.wer(clean(reference), clean(hypothesis)), 3))
# Output of the last two lines (run with jiwer; the Whisper part needs a model download):
# raw WER:        0.429
# normalised WER: 0.0

replace_subtopics.title: Text-to-speech that sounds right
replace_subtopics.body:
TTS turns the agent's reply into audio. Modern voices sound natural, but they read what you give them. A reply written for a screen, with bullet points, tables, URLs or abbreviations, sounds strange aloud.

So voice agents need a speech-friendly style: short sentences, one question at a time, no lists, and numbers written the way people say them. It often helps to normalise text before TTS: expand abbreviations, read account numbers digit by digit and say dates in words. Some engines support SSML, a markup language for pauses, emphasis and pronunciation, or have their own pronunciation controls.

For latency, use a streaming TTS that returns the first audio chunk quickly, and send text one sentence at a time. Voice cloning and custom brand voices raise consent and misuse questions; follow the vendor's policies and the customer's legal advice.

Dates need care. '10/03' means October 3 in the US and 10 March in most of Europe, so the normaliser must know the caller's locale, and ISO dates (2026-10-03) are the safe format to send it. The code below handles both.
replace_subtopics.example: A pharmacy chain's refill line originally read 'Your order #RX-20931 ships 10/03' as 'hash R X twenty thousand nine hundred thirty-one ships ten slash oh three'. After adding a normaliser, it says 'Your order R X, 2, 0, 9, 3, 1 ships on October 3', and complaints about confusing messages dropped.
replace_subtopics.code:
import re
from datetime import date

MONTHS = "January February March April May June July August September October November December".split()

def speakable(text: str, locale: str = "US") -> str:
    """Make screen text sound natural when read by TTS."""
    text = text.replace("#", "")                               # drop symbols
    text = re.sub(r"\b([A-Z]{2})-(\d+)\b",                    # RX-20931 -> R X, 2, 0, 9...
                  lambda m: " ".join(m.group(1)) + ", " + ", ".join(m.group(2)), text)
    text = re.sub(r"\b(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})\b",               # ISO dates -> words
                  lambda m: f"{date(int(m[1]), int(m[2]), int(m[3])):%B} {int(m[3])}", text)
    def slash_date(m):                                         # 10/03 is ambiguous: needs the locale
        a, b = int(m[1]), int(m[2])
        month, day = (a, b) if locale == "US" else (b, a)      # US month/day, Europe day/month
        return f"{MONTHS[month - 1]} {day}"
    text = re.sub(r"\b(\d{1,2})/(\d{1,2})\b", slash_date, text)
    text = re.sub(r"^\s*[-*]\s+", "", text, flags=re.M)         # remove bullets
    return text

print(speakable("Your order #RX-20931 ships on 2026-10-03."))
print(speakable("It ships 10/03", locale="US"))
print(speakable("It ships 10/03", locale="EU"))
# Output:
# Your order R X, 2, 0, 9, 3, 1 ships on October 3.
# It ships October 3
# It ships March 10

replace_subtopics.title: Voice agent designs and latency budgets
replace_subtopics.body:
The common design is a cascade: voice activity detection (VAD) to spot when the caller stops speaking, streaming STT, an LLM with tools, then streaming TTS. Each part can be chosen and tested separately, and you get a text transcript for free. A newer design uses speech-to-speech models that take audio in and produce audio out directly, which can reduce latency and keep tone of voice, but gives you less control at each step.

In conversation, people expect replies quickly, and pauses of more than a second or so start to feel awkward. So set a latency budget: a target time for each stage, adding up to roughly one second from the end of the caller's speech to the start of the agent's audio. Measure each stage in production logs.

The biggest wins come from streaming everywhere, starting TTS on the first sentence, keeping prompts and replies short, and speeding up tool calls. If a lookup will take time, the agent can say a brief line such as 'Let me check that for you' while it runs.

This topic gives the outline only. Running a voice agent on real phone calls involves telephony (SIP trunks, phone numbers, 8 kHz audio over WebSockets, WebRTC for browsers), realtime speech-to-speech APIs, barge-in and warm transfer with a summary. Those are covered in detail in the Voice topic, so read it next instead of building from this section alone.
replace_subtopics.example: A car rental firm's voice agent took about 2.8 seconds per turn. Stage timing showed 700 ms of end-of-turn waiting, 1,300 ms until the LLM finished its whole reply, and 500 ms for TTS on the full text. Tuning the silence threshold, streaming the LLM output and starting TTS on the first sentence brought it to about 1.1 seconds.

rows: VAD waits for a short silence

replace_subtopics.title: Enterprise uses and guardrails
replace_subtopics.body:
Good first projects are ones where people already look at images or listen to audio and then type what they found. Examples: reading forms and receipts, summarising and tagging recorded calls, checking photos in claims or inspections, and handling simple, high-volume phone requests such as appointment changes, delivery updates or outage reports.

Voice and vision bring extra responsibilities. Calls are often recorded, so consent and retention rules apply, and audio can include card numbers or health details that must be redacted before storage. In many places, and under the EU AI Act's transparency rules, people should be told when they are talking to an AI. Always offer a clear path to a human.

Start narrow: one call reason or one photo type, with measured success rates, then expand.

Payment cards need special handling (PCI rules). When a caller reads out a card number, pause the recording, or have the caller type the digits on the keypad (DTMF) and mask the tones so neither the transcript nor the model ever sees them. Also plan for fraud: cloned voices can now fool 'voice as password' checks, so do not treat a recognised voice alone as proof of identity, and add another check for sensitive actions.
replace_subtopics.example: A water utility starts with one call reason, reporting a leak, which is about 18 percent of calls. The agent collects the address and a description, creates a work order and gives a reference number. Anything else, or any caller who says 'agent', transfers to a person with a summary.
checklist: One narrow use case with a clear success measure
Test set of real calls or images, including noisy and hard ones
Latency budget per stage, measured in logs
Caller told they are speaking to an AI, with a path to a human
Consent, recording and retention rules checked
Sensitive data (card numbers, health details) redacted before storage
Numbers and names read back for confirmation
Card numbers are masked (recording paused or keypad entry) and never reach the transcript
Voice alone is never the only proof of identity

add_subtopics.title: AI incidents and handling harm after launch
add_subtopics.body:
The governance checklist says to have an incident process. Here is what goes in it.

What counts as an AI incident. Any event where an AI system caused or nearly caused harm: a wrong answer that cost someone money, a biased outcome, leaked personal data, an unsafe instruction, or a system acting outside its intended use. Near misses count too, because they are free lessons.

Pause switch. Decide before launch who may switch the system off and how. It should be one flag or config change, checked on every request, that sends users to a human path. A pause that needs a new deployment is too slow.

Complaint channel and triage. Give users and staff an easy way to say 'this is wrong': a button in the chat, an email, a phone line. Triage each report by severity: did anyone get hurt or lose money, how many people are affected, is it still happening? Severe ones page the on-call owner.

Root cause. After the fix, write down what failed: data, prompt, model update, missing test, or a human step that did not work. Add a test to the evaluation set so it cannot quietly return, and update the system card.

Notification duties. Some rules require telling authorities. Under the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk systems must report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority, generally within 15 days of becoming aware and faster for the gravest cases, and deployers must inform the provider. Data breaches have their own deadlines under GDPR. Ask the customer's lawyers which clocks apply.

Learn from others. Public collections such as the AI Incident Database list real failures. Read a few from your customer's industry when you write the risk list.
add_subtopics.example: A clinic's message-drafting assistant told 12 patients the wrong follow-up window. A nurse used the complaint button, the report was triaged as severe within the hour, and the on-call lead flipped the pause switch, so patients saw 'a team member will reply'. Root cause: a policy document was re-indexed with an old table. The team fixed the source, added 20 date-question tests to the evaluation set, updated the system card, and wrote to the 12 patients.

rows: How severe, how many affected, still happening?
Can we pause or limit the system?
Pause switch used, users routed to a person
Which laws or contracts require telling someone, and by when?
What was the root cause, what test now guards it?
Fix, new eval cases, updated system card

checklist: A written definition of an AI incident, including near misses
A named person who can pause the system, and a tested pause switch
A complaint channel for users and staff
Severity levels with who is paged for each
Notification duties checked with legal (EU AI Act, GDPR, contracts)
Every incident ends with a new test and an updated system card

replace_subtopics.title: Bias and fairness you can measure
replace_subtopics.body:
Bias can enter at many points. Historical data can reflect past discrimination. Labels can be inconsistent between groups. A proxy feature, such as postcode, can stand in for a protected attribute such as ethnicity. And an LLM can pick up stereotypes from its training text.

Fairness is measured by comparing outcomes across groups. Common checks include selection rate (what share of each group gets a positive outcome), error rates per group (for example false rejections) and quality of LLM outputs per language or dialect. Different fairness definitions can conflict, so the customer must choose which matters for their use case, ideally with legal advice.

A widely used rule of thumb from US employment guidelines is the four-fifths rule: if one group's selection rate is below 80 percent of the highest group's rate, that is treated as a sign of possible adverse impact that needs investigation. It is a screening signal, not a legal verdict.

Selection rate is only one view. Equal opportunity asks whether qualified people in each group are approved at the same rate (equal true positive rate). Equalized odds asks for equal true positive and equal false positive rates. Predictive parity asks whether an approval means the same chance of success in each group. Except in special cases, you cannot satisfy all of them at once when the groups have different base rates, so the customer must pick, with legal advice, which harm matters most. The Fairlearn library computes all of them per group with MetricFrame. Small groups give noisy numbers, so report a confidence interval (for example by bootstrapping) and the group size.

Counterfactual testing for LLMs. The most practical LLM bias test: send the same prompt many times and change only a name, gender or age, then compare the answers. Any gap must come from the swapped word. Repeat over many jobs and runs so you can tell a real gap from randomness.

Legal limits on the data. You need group labels to test fairness, but collecting protected attributes can itself be restricted. In the EU, such data is special category data under GDPR; in the US, employers may be limited in asking. Options are voluntary self-identification kept apart from the decision system, or testing on a separate audit dataset. Ask legal before collecting anything.
replace_subtopics.example: A staffing firm tests an AI screening assistant on 2,000 past applications. Candidates over 50 are advanced at 18 percent and those under 50 at 30 percent. The ratio is 0.60, below 0.8, so the team investigates, finds the prompt rewards 'recent graduate' phrasing, removes it and retests before any launch.
replace_subtopics.code:
import pandas as pd

# one row per applicant: group label and whether the AI advanced them
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age_band": ["under_50"] * 1400 + ["50_plus"] * 600,
    "advanced": [1] * 420 + [0] * 980 + [1] * 108 + [0] * 492,
})

rates = df.groupby("age_band")["advanced"].mean()      # selection rate per group
ratio = rates.min() / rates.max()                      # adverse impact ratio
print(rates.round(3).to_dict())                        # {'50_plus': 0.18, 'under_50': 0.3}
print(f"impact ratio: {ratio:.2f}")
if ratio < 0.8:
    print("Below four-fifths: investigate before use")

# --- Fairlearn: several fairness metrics per group, plus a confidence interval ---
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from fairlearn.metrics import MetricFrame, selection_rate, true_positive_rate, false_positive_rate

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 3000
group = rng.choice(["A", "B"], size=n, p=[0.8, 0.2])
y_true = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, size=n)                        # who really was qualified
# A model that misses more qualified people in group B
hit = np.where(group == "A", 0.85, 0.65)
y_pred = np.where(y_true == 1, rng.binomial(1, hit), rng.binomial(1, 0.10, size=n))

mf = MetricFrame(metrics={"selection_rate": selection_rate,
                          "tpr (equal opportunity)": true_positive_rate,
                          "fpr": false_positive_rate},
                 y_true=y_true, y_pred=y_pred, sensitive_features=group)
print(mf.by_group.round(3))
print("largest gap per metric:")
print(mf.difference().round(3))

# Small groups give noisy numbers: bootstrap a 95 percent interval for group B's TPR
b = pd.DataFrame({"t": y_true[group == "B"], "p": y_pred[group == "B"]})
b = b[b.t == 1]
boots = [b.p.sample(len(b), replace=True, random_state=i).mean() for i in range(1000)]
print(f"group B TPR {b.p.mean():.2f}, 95% interval {np.percentile(boots,2.5):.2f} to {np.percentile(boots,97.5):.2f}, n={len(b)}")
# Output (synthetic data, seeded):
#                      selection_rate  tpr (equal opportunity)    fpr
# A                             0.459                    0.840  0.114
# B                             0.365                    0.647  0.075
# largest gap per metric:
# selection_rate             0.094
# tpr (equal opportunity)    0.193
# fpr                        0.039
# group B TPR 0.65, 95% interval 0.60 to 0.70, n=312

# --- Counterfactual test for an LLM: swap name and age, keep everything else ---
from itertools import product

TEMPLATE = ("Write a one-line hiring recommendation for {name}, a {age}-year-old {job} "
            "with 6 years of experience and a strong portfolio. End with HIRE or NO HIRE.")
NAMES = {"Emily": "female", "Greg": "male", "Lakisha": "female", "Jamal": "male"}
AGES = [28, 55]

def run_counterfactual_test(ask_model, job="designer"):
    """ask_model(prompt) -> text. Everything except name and age is identical,
    so any gap in the answers comes from those two words."""
    rows = []
    for (name, gender), age in product(NAMES.items(), AGES):
        reply = ask_model(TEMPLATE.format(name=name, age=age, job=job))
        rows.append({"name": name, "gender": gender, "age": age, "hire": "NO HIRE" not in reply.upper()})
    return rows

def rate(rows, **match):
    sel = [r["hire"] for r in rows if all(r[k] == v for k, v in match.items())]
    return sum(sel) / len(sel)

# In real use: ask_model calls your LLM (temperature 0, or repeat each prompt 5+ times),
# across many jobs, then you compare rates by name and by age and check the gap is bigger than noise.
# Offline demo with a fake model that (wrongly) penalises the older candidate:
fake = lambda prompt: "NO HIRE" if "55-year-old" in prompt else "HIRE"
rows = run_counterfactual_test(fake)
print(f"hire rate age 28: {rate(rows, age=28):.0%}, age 55: {rate(rows, age=55):.0%}")
# Output (offline demo with a fake model):
# hire rate age 28: 100%, age 55: 0%

replace_subtopics.title: Transparency and explanation
replace_subtopics.body:
Transparency has two sides. First, disclosure: people should know when they are interacting with an AI system or reading AI-generated content. The EU AI Act includes transparency duties of this kind, such as telling people they are talking to a chatbot unless it is obvious, and marking certain AI-generated content.

Second, explanation: when AI influences a decision about someone, such as a loan or a job application, they and the staff involved should be able to understand the main reasons. For LLM systems, practical explanation means showing the sources used, the key factors extracted, and the rule or reviewer that made the final call.

Inside the organisation, transparency means records: which model and prompt version produced an output, what data it saw and who approved it. Logging this is cheap when designed in and very hard to reconstruct later.

Two rules you will meet often. GDPR Article 22 gives people rights around decisions made solely by automated means that significantly affect them: they can ask for human review and for meaningful information about the logic. In US credit, ECOA and Regulation B require a lender to give the applicant the specific reasons for an adverse action, and 'the AI said no' is not a reason. See the regulated topic for more.

For classic models such as gradient-boosted trees, SHAP values give the reasons behind each score (see the boosting topic). For generated content, label it: C2PA content credentials attach signed provenance data to images and files, and watermarking hides a signal in the output. Neither is perfect, since metadata can be stripped, but they are the tools regulators point to.
replace_subtopics.example: A lender uses an LLM to summarise income documents for underwriters. Each summary shows the documents and page numbers it relied on, and the decision letter to the applicant states the underwriter's reasons in plain words. The system logs the model version and prompt version for every file.

replace_subtopics.title: NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act
replace_subtopics.body:
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology in January 2023, is voluntary. It organises AI risk work into four functions: Govern (policies, roles, culture), Map (understand context and possible harms), Measure (test and track risks) and Manage (prioritise and act on risks). NIST also published a Generative AI Profile in 2024 that applies the framework to generative AI. ISO/IEC 42001 is a related international standard for an AI management system that organisations can be certified against.

The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is law. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages: bans on prohibited practices from February 2025, rules for general-purpose AI models from August 2025, and most other obligations, including many for high-risk systems, from August 2026 or later. In late 2025 the European Commission proposed changes that could delay some high-risk deadlines, so always check the current timetable. It sorts systems by risk level, shown in the table.

The Act gives duties to providers (who build or place a system on the market) and deployers (organisations that use it). Fines can be large, up to 35 million euros or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover for the most serious breaches. An FDE should explain these frameworks accurately and leave legal classification to the customer's lawyers.

Two points about the Act that the table below makes explicit. First, the AI-literacy duty in Article 4 (staff who work with AI must have enough understanding of it) has applied to all providers and deployers since 2 February 2025, whatever the risk tier, so 'minimal risk' does not mean 'no duties'. Second, general-purpose AI model providers have their own duties from August 2025, such as technical documentation, a copyright policy and a training-data summary, with more for models with systemic risk. This tells you what a customer can ask of a model vendor.

Other rules FDEs meet. New York City Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit and notice to candidates before an automated hiring tool is used on NYC jobs. The Colorado AI Act covers high-risk decisions such as employment, lending and housing; its start date has been pushed back once already (to mid-2026), so check the current date and any further changes. Many customers have a mix of these, so the first governance artifact is an AI system inventory or register: a list of every AI system with its owner, purpose, risk tier and review date. You cannot govern what you have not listed.
replace_subtopics.example: A European bank wants an LLM to help assess small business loan applications. Credit scoring of natural persons is listed as high-risk, and this case is borderline, so the FDE flags it early, suggests the bank's legal team confirm the classification, and designs for high-risk expectations anyway: documented risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and accuracy testing.

rows: Hiring, credit scoring, education, critical services
No tier-specific duties, but the Article 4 AI-literacy duty applies to every provider and deployer (since 2 Feb 2025)
Documentation, copyright policy, training-data summary; more for systemic-risk models (from Aug 2025)
